title: A 3 A.M. Caller Claiming To Be My Grandson Begged Me For $8,500 In Bail After An Accident In Mexico, Using His Exact Voice, His Dog’s Name, And A Childhood Nickname Only Family Knew, And A Young Pharmacy Clerk Stopped Me Before I Bought The
excerpt: I am seventy-nine years old. I have lived in the same little house in Carmel, Indiana, for forty-one years. My husband George passed six years ago. I have three children, seven grandchildren, and one very spoiled beagle named Pickles.
author: admin

blocks.text: PART 1 — THE CALL AT 2:14 A.M.

I am seventy-nine years old. I have lived in the same little house in Carmel, Indiana, for forty-one years. My husband George passed six years ago. I have three children, seven grandchildren, and one very spoiled beagle named Pickles.

I am not a foolish woman. I balanced the books for a Methodist church for twenty-two years. I read the scam warnings in the church bulletin. I had heard about grandparent scams at a senior center talk just the spring before.
So I want you to understand that when my phone rang at 2:14 on a Thursday morning, I was not an easy mark. I was simply a grandmother who loved her grandson.
“Grandma?” a young man’s voice said. “Grandma, it’s me. It’s Bug.”

Only my family calls my grandson Evan “Bug.” He got the nickname when he was three and refused to wear anything but a ladybug raincoat for an entire summer. He is twenty now, a junior studying engineering at a university in Ohio, and he still lets me call him Bug when nobody else is around.
“Evan?” I sat straight up in bed. “Honey, what’s wrong?”
He was crying. It was his voice. I would have bet my life on it. It had that little crack in it he has had since his voice changed, and the way he says “Grandma” with the second syllable higher.

“I’m in trouble,” he said. “I’m so stupid. I went to Mexico with some guys for a long weekend. There was an accident. I was driving. A woman got hurt. They arrested me. Grandma, please, please don’t tell Mom. She’ll kill me.”
My heart was pounding so hard I could feel it in my ears.

“I’m okay. I hit my knee on the dashboard, right on my old scar. The lady’s going to be okay too, I think. But I need bail. They said if I don’t post bail by morning, they’ll transfer me to a prison and I could be there for weeks.”
He knew about his scar. The one he got falling off his bike at age seven, in my driveway, while I was supposed to be watching him.
PART 2 — THE LAWYER ON THE LINE
Before I could ask another question, a different voice came on the line. An older man, calm and professional, with a slight accent.
“Mrs. Whitaker, my name is Robert Delgado. I’m an attorney working with the American consulate to help your grandson. I want you to know Evan is safe. He is frightened, but he is safe.”

He explained very patiently. The bail was $8,500. Because of the time difference and the weekend, the courts in that part of Mexico could not take bank transfers. The fastest and safest way was to purchase prepaid cards, read him the numbers, and he would pay the court directly.
“There is also a gag order on the case,” he said. “It is very important that you do not discuss this with anyone, even your family, or it could jeopardize Evan’s release. Do you understand?”
Somewhere in the back of my mind, a little bell rang. Gift cards. Secrecy. The senior center talk.
“I want to speak to my grandson again,” I said.
There was a pause, and then Evan was back, still crying.
“Grandma, please. I’m so scared. Please just do what he says. And Grandma? Don’t let Pickles sleep on the bed. You know she always snores.”
I laughed through my tears, because it was such an Evan thing to say. Pickles was, at that very moment, snoring at the foot of my bed.
The little bell in my head went quiet. Scammers do not know the name of your dog. Scammers do not know that she snores.
“Okay,” I said. “Okay, honey. Grandma’s going to take care of it.”

Mr. Delgado came back on. He told me exactly which store to go to: the twenty-four-hour drugstore on Range Line Road, two miles from my house. He knew where I lived. He told me to buy cards from several different brands so the purchases would not get flagged. He said to keep the phone line open in my pocket and call him back the moment I had them.
I put on my bathrobe and my coat over it, grabbed my purse and car keys, and drove through the empty streets in the dark.
PART 3 — THE CLERK NAMED DARIUS
The drugstore was bright and empty at three in the morning. Fluorescent lights hummed. A radio was playing soft rock very quietly.
There was one employee at the register, a young man maybe twenty-three, tall, with glasses and a name tag that said Darius. He was restocking cough drops.

I went straight to the gift card rack near the front. I started pulling cards off the hooks. Five hundred dollars here. Two hundred there. My hands were shaking so badly I dropped two of them on the floor.
Darius came over and picked them up for me. He looked at the stack in my hands. Then he looked at my face, my bathrobe under my coat, my slippers.
“Ma’am,” he said gently, “that’s a lot of gift cards. Are you okay?”
“I’m fine,” I said, too quickly. “They’re presents.”
He nodded slowly. Then he asked, in the same calm, kind voice, “Ma’am, who told you to buy these?”
“Is it a grandkid?” he asked softly. “Somebody in trouble? Jail, maybe? An accident?”

“Because I’ve seen it before,” he said. “Four times in the last year, right here at this counter. It’s always somebody’s grandma, always the middle of the night, always gift cards. And they always say not to tell anybody.”
“It was his voice,” I whispered. “I swear to you. It was really his voice.” > “I believe you,” Darius said. “They can do that now. That’s what makes it so cruel.”
He asked me if I had my grandson’s real phone number. I did, of course. He asked me to call it, right there, with him standing beside me.
My hands were shaking too hard to dial. Darius did it for me, reading the numbers off my phone.
It rang four times. Then a groggy voice answered.
“Grandma? Is everything okay? It’s three in the morning.”
It was Evan. Asleep in his dorm room in Ohio. He had never been to Mexico in his life.
PART 4 — ON THE FLOOR OF THE DRUGSTORE
I don’t remember sitting down. Darius told me later that my knees just folded and I sat down on the floor right there by the gift card rack, with my back against a display of reading glasses.
I was crying so hard I couldn’t talk. Evan was on the phone, wide awake now and frightened, saying, “Grandma? Grandma, what’s going on? Who is with you?”

Darius took the phone gently and explained everything to him. Then he brought me a bottle of water and a folding chair from the back room and sat down on the floor next to me until I could breathe again.
My other phone, the one with the scammer’s call still open in my coat pocket, buzzed. Darius took it out, looked at it, and hung up.
“You don’t owe them another word,” he said.

Darius waited with me until my daughter Karen, Evan’s mother, arrived twenty minutes later. He had found her number in my phone and called her himself. Karen ran into the store in pajama pants and a parka and wrapped her arms around me.
I had not spent a single dollar. Darius had stopped me before anything was paid for. The cards were still sitting in a pile on the counter, never activated.
I came within one minute of losing $8,500 to people who had stolen my grandson’s voice. A young man earning hourly wages at three in the morning cared enough to ask me one simple question.
Before we left, I tried to give Darius some money from my purse. He refused. I asked for his manager’s name so I could write a letter. He smiled and wrote it down on the back of a receipt.
“Just tell your friends,” he said. “Tell every grandma you know. That’s the only thing that stops it.”
I promised him I would. That is part of why I am writing this.
PART 5 — THE QUESTION THAT KEPT ME AWAKE

The next morning, my daughter and I filed a police report with the Carmel Police Department and a report online with the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center. A detective named Sergeant Paula Reyes came to my house that afternoon.

She was very kind. She told me that what happened to me was becoming more common. Criminals can now use short clips of someone’s voice, from social media videos or voicemail greetings, and computer programs to create a convincing copy of that voice.
“They only need a few seconds of audio,” she said. “Sometimes less. And many of these calls are live, with someone typing what the fake voice should say.”
